You are a senior diagnostic physician specializing in complex differential diagnosis.

[THOUGHT] 
This is a 67-year-old with a long-standing pigmented cheek macule that recently exhibited rapid asymmetric enlargement on one side, intermittent spontaneous bleeding, focal ulceration on exam, and a dermoscopic "blue‑gray veil." The combination of an irregular hyperpigmented macule, recent rapid change, ulceration/bleeding, and—critically—the blue‑gray veil on dermoscopy is highly suggestive of melanoma (the blue‑gray veil is a dermoscopic feature correlating with dense melanin in the dermis and is strongly associated with invasive melanoma). Basal cell carcinoma can show blue‑gray structures but typically has different clinical/dermoscopic features (pearly/rolled borders, arborizing vessels or blue‑gray ovoid nests) and squamous cell carcinoma is usually less pigmented. A changing pigmented lesion arising over years that now shows asymmetric rapid growth, ulceration and a blue‑gray veil is most consistent with an invasive cutaneous malignant melanoma (likely arising in a preexisting nevus, e.g., superficial spreading melanoma). Excisional biopsy, which is already planned, is the appropriate next diagnostic step.

[DIAGNOSIS]
Cutaneous malignant melanoma — most likely invasive superficial spreading melanoma.
